questions.stem: How does Object-Oriented Data Modelling represent data?
options: As objects that combine attributes (data) and methods (behaviour)
As rows and columns governed by functional dependencies
As owner–member sets linked by pointers
As immutable events in an append-only log
As key–value pairs optimised for lookup
questions.explanation: Object-oriented modelling treats real-world entities as self-contained units that include both state and behaviour, mirroring object-oriented programming.

questions.stem: What was the original goal of object-oriented data modelling?
options: To maximise analytical query performance
To align persistent storage directly with object-oriented application design, removing the need to transform objects into relational tables
To enforce Third Normal Form in application code
To support horizontal scale-out across distributed nodes
To provide a semantic layer for reasoning
questions.explanation: The goal was to align storage with object-oriented application design so objects would not need to be transformed into relational tables.

questions.stem: In an object-oriented model, which method might a LoanApplication class define?
options: calculateRisk()
normalise()
partitionByCustomer()
approve()
traverseSet()
questions.explanation: A LoanApplication object may include attributes such as LoanID, Amount, InterestRate and Status together with methods like approve() or reject(); calculateRisk() belongs to Customer.

questions.stem: How are relationships between entities expressed in object-oriented data modelling?
options: Through foreign keys
Through owner–member sets
Through object references
Through shared partition keys
Through fact-table joins
questions.explanation: Relationships are expressed through object references rather than foreign keys, and inheritance lets specialised types extend base classes.

questions.stem: Which products are named as Object-Oriented Database Management Systems from the late 1980s and 1990s?
options: Hibernate, Entity Framework and Spring
MongoDB, Couchbase and Redis
IMS, IDMS and DB2
Neo4j, Cassandra and Bigtable
ObjectStore, GemStone and Versant
questions.explanation: OODBMS products such as ObjectStore, GemStone and Versant gained attention in the late 1980s and 1990s, with standards like ODMG-93 attempting to formalise the practice.

questions.stem: What largely overtook pure object databases by the early 2000s?
options: Relational databases combined with Object-Relational Mapping frameworks such as Hibernate and Entity Framework
Hierarchical mainframe databases
Graph databases
Wide-column stores
Event-streaming platforms
questions.explanation: ORM frameworks let developers keep object-oriented programming practices while storing data in relational systems, displacing pure object databases.

questions.stem: In the loan approval scenario, when do the limitations of an object database become evident?
options: When storing a single LoanApplication object
When the organisation needs large-scale reporting, regulatory analytics or cross-portfolio aggregation
When adding a new attribute to the Customer class
When invoking the approve() method
When defining inheritance between loan types
questions.explanation: Analytical workloads demand declarative querying, flexible joins and optimised aggregations, which are strengths of relational systems rather than object databases.

questions.stem: Why do normalisation forms not directly apply to object-oriented data modelling?
options: Because object databases store only unstructured data
Because objects are always stored in 6NF
Because objects are not structured as relational tables governed by functional dependencies; design is driven by class hierarchies and behaviour encapsulation
Because object databases forbid primary keys
Because object databases only support analytical workloads
questions.explanation: Normal forms are relational constructs; object-oriented design is driven by class hierarchies and encapsulation rather than relational integrity rules.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a challenge of object-oriented data modelling?
options: Query capabilities that are more procedural and less flexible than SQL
Difficulty supporting analytical use cases efficiently
Limited interoperability across systems compared with relational standards
Inability to express inheritance between classes
Being largely obsolete as a standalone database paradigm
questions.explanation: Support for inheritance, encapsulation and polymorphism is an advantage of object-oriented modelling; its challenges are procedural querying, weak analytics and limited interoperability.

questions.stem: Where does the influence of object-oriented data modelling persist today?
options: In hierarchical directory services
In CODASYL network databases
In Domain–Key Normal Form
In star schema fact tables
In document databases with nested JSON structures and in API payloads that mirror object models
questions.explanation: Modern document databases with nested JSON reflect object-style thinking and API payloads often mirror object models, so the paradigm served as a bridge between programming and persistence.
